title: Conservation of Energy
lead: Energy is conserved: whatever forms it passes through, the total at the end of a process is the total it began with. This section states that law, adds one term to the mechanical energy and the nonconservative work for every other kind of energy a system holds, names the forms energy takes beyond the mechanical ones, follows energy through the conversions that are going on all the time, and defines the efficiency of a conversion as the share of the energy put in that comes out as useful work.
objectives: Explain the law of the conservation of energy.
Describe some of the many forms of energy.
Define efficiency of an energy conversion process as the fraction left as useful energy or work, rather than being transformed, for example, into thermal energy.
summary_html:
• The law of conservation of energy states that the total energy is constant in any process. Energy may change in form or be transferred from one system to another, but the total remains the same.
  • When all forms of energy are considered, conservation of energy is written in equation form as $\kKEi + \kPEi + \kWnc + \kOEi = \kKEf + \kPEf + \kOEf$, where $\kOE$ is all other forms of energy besides mechanical energy.
  • Commonly encountered forms of energy include electric energy, chemical energy, radiant energy, nuclear energy, and thermal energy.
  • Energy is often utilized to do work, but it is not possible to convert all the energy of a system to work.
  • The efficiency $\text{Eff}$ of a machine or human is defined to be $\text{Eff} = \frac{\kWout}{\kEin}$, where $\kWout$ is useful work output and $\kEin$ is the energy consumed.

exercises.prompt: You do 30 J of work to load a toy dart gun. However, the dart is 10 cm long and feels a frictional force of 10 N while going through the dart gun’s barrel. What is the kinetic energy of the fired dart?

answer.hint: The work you did to load the gun is stored in the spring, and friction acts on the dart over the length of the barrel, so write the account with a term for the work done against friction.

exercises.prompt: When an object is lifted by a crane, it begins and ends its motion at rest. The same is true of an object pushed across a rough surface. Explain why this happens. What are the differences between these systems?

answer.solution: In both cases the object is at rest at the beginning and at rest at the end, so its kinetic energy is the same at both instants and the change in kinetic energy over the whole motion is zero. By the work-energy theorem the net work done on the object is therefore zero, even though work has certainly been done: the crane’s cable does positive work on the load while gravity does an equal amount of negative work, and the push does positive work on the object while friction does an equal amount of negative work. The difference between the two systems is where the energy has gone. Gravity is a conservative force, so the work done against it is stored as gravitational potential energy and can be had back by lowering the load; the load is higher than it was and the mechanical energy of the load-Earth system has risen by exactly the work the crane did. Friction is nonconservative, so the work done against it has left as thermal energy in the surface and in the object, and no change of position will give it back; the mechanical energy of that system is what it was, and the energy the push put in is other energy now.

exercises.prompt: A child has two red wagons, with the rear one tied to the front by a stretchy rope (a spring). If the child pulls on the front wagon, the ____ increases.

options: potential energy stored in the spring
answer.hint: Ask what the child’s work goes into: the wagons are moving faster than they were, and the rope between them is stretched further than it was.

exercises.prompt: A child has two red wagons, with the rear one tied to the front by a stretchy rope (a spring). If the child pulls on the front wagon, the energy stored in the system increases. How do the relative amounts of potential and kinetic energy in this system change over time?

answer.solution: At the first tug the front wagon moves before the rear one does, so the rope stretches and most of the energy the child has put in is potential energy stored in the rope, while the rear wagon is still nearly at rest. The stretched rope then pulls the rear wagon forward: the stretch falls and the wagon speeds up, so the potential energy stored in the rope is converted into the kinetic energy of the wagons. Because the rope is a spring, the rear wagon overshoots, the rope goes slack, and the rear wagon then falls behind again and stretches it once more, so the two forms trade back and forth as the pair rolls along. The total keeps rising, since the child keeps doing work on the front wagon, but at any one moment how it is split depends on how far the rope happens to be stretched. Friction in the wheels and losses in the rope itself turn part of the total into thermal energy while the trading goes on, so the share that is mechanical falls the longer the pull lasts.

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following are closed systems?
  1. Earth
  2. a car
  3. a frictionless pendulum
  4. a mass on a spring in a vacuum
Describe a real-world example of a closed system.

answer.solution: Look for something across whose boundary no energy passes: nothing is put in and nothing leaks out. Nothing in the world is perfectly closed, so any real example is an approximation over a stretch of time short enough that what does cross the boundary does not matter. A vacuum flask of hot coffee with its stopper in is a good one, because the vacuum between its walls carries away almost no thermal energy, so the energy inside it is very nearly constant for an hour or two. A heavy bob swinging on a long wire inside a sealed and evacuated case is another, since there is no air to rub against and little friction at the support. The Earth is often offered and is a poor choice, because the Sun pours radiant energy onto it all day and the Earth radiates energy back into space all night. Whichever example you choose, say where the boundary of your system is and what would have to cross it for the system to stop being closed.

exercises.prompt: A 5.0-kg rock falls off of a 10 m cliff. If air resistance exerts an average force of 10 N, what is the kinetic energy when the rock hits the ground?

answer.hint: The potential energy the rock loses is $mgh$, and air resistance takes a force multiplied by the same distance away from it; one of the four options is not even an energy.

exercises.prompt: Hydroelectricity is generated by storing water behind a dam, and then letting some of it run through generators in the dam to turn them. If the system is the water, what is the environment that is doing work on it? If a dam has water 100 m deep behind it, how much energy was generated if 10,000 kg of water exited the dam at 2.0 m/s?

answer.solution: The environment doing work on the water is the Earth, through the gravitational force: as the water falls the gravitational potential energy of the water-Earth system is converted, which is the same thing as saying that gravity does work on the water. For the second part, take the water 100 m up behind the dam as the initial state and the water leaving the outlet at 2.0 m/s as the final state, and write the account. Its potential energy at the start, measured from the outlet, is $\kPEg = m\kg\kh = (10{,}000\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)(100\ \text{m})$, and it starts at rest, so that is all the energy it has. The energy it still carries as it leaves is $\kKE = \tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(10{,}000\ \text{kg})(2.0\ \text{m/s})^2$. Whatever the water no longer has, the generators have taken, so the energy generated is the first of those numbers less the second, and less again whatever friction in the pipes turned into thermal energy on the way down, which the question gives you no way to work out and asks you to neglect.

exercises.prompt: Consider the following scenario. A car for which friction is not negligible accelerates from rest down a hill, running out of gasoline after a short distance. The driver lets the car coast farther down the hill, then up and over a small crest. He then coasts down that hill into a gas station, where he brakes to a stop and fills the tank with gasoline. Identify the forms of energy the car has, and how they are changed and transferred in this series of events.

answer.solution: Follow the car through the run and name what it has at every stage. At the top it is at rest, so it has gravitational potential energy and no kinetic energy, and the gasoline in its tank carries chemical energy. As it accelerates down the first hill the engine turns part of that chemical energy into the kinetic energy of the car, the potential energy of the car-Earth system falls into kinetic energy as well, and friction in the drivetrain and the tires and the drag of the air turn part of both into thermal energy, which warms the car and the air. When the gasoline runs out there is no chemical energy left to draw on, and from there the only exchange is between gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, less what friction keeps taking. Coasting up over the crest the car gives kinetic energy back as potential energy and slows; running down the second hill it takes it back again and speeds up. Braking at the gas station turns all of the kinetic energy that is left into thermal energy in the brakes. Filling the tank transfers chemical energy into the car from outside it, which is a transfer between systems rather than a change of form. At no stage is any energy lost: what one form gives up another has taken.

exercises.prompt: Describe the energy transfers and transformations for a javelin, starting from the point at which an athlete picks up the javelin and ending when the javelin is stuck into the ground after being thrown.

answer.solution: The chemical energy in the athlete’s muscles is the source of all of it. Picking the javelin up and carrying it to the mark, the athlete converts a little of that chemical energy into the gravitational potential energy of the raised javelin and into the kinetic energy of the run-up, and most of it into thermal energy in the athlete’s body, since a body is only about a fifth efficient. In the throw the athlete does work on the javelin over the length of the arm and the turn of the body, so more chemical energy becomes the kinetic energy the javelin leaves with. In flight the javelin trades kinetic energy for gravitational potential energy as it rises and takes it back as it falls, while the air resistance on it turns a small part of the total into thermal energy in the javelin and the air. When the point strikes the ground the javelin’s kinetic energy goes into the work of pushing the soil apart, into thermal energy in the soil and the shaft, and into the sound of the impact. The javelin ends at rest and lower than it was thrown, and every joule it began with is somewhere else.

exercises.prompt: Do devices with efficiencies of less than one violate the law of conservation of energy? Explain.

answer.solution: No. An efficiency of less than one says that only part of the energy put in comes out as useful work, not that the rest of it has gone away. The conservation law is about the total, and the total is the same as it was: what does not come out as useful work leaves as thermal energy in the device and the air around it, and as sound and light. A gasoline engine whose efficiency is 30 percent turns three tenths of the chemical energy in its fuel into the work of driving the car, and the other seven tenths leaves through the radiator and the exhaust pipe as thermal energy. The efficiency counts only the useful share; the conservation law counts every joule.

exercises.prompt: List four different forms or types of energy. Give one example of a conversion from each of these forms to another form.

answer.solution: Electrical energy, chemical energy, radiant energy, nuclear energy and thermal energy are five of the forms this section names, and any four of them will do. Electrical energy is converted into the mechanical energy of a turning shaft in an electric motor. Chemical energy in gasoline is converted into thermal energy and then into mechanical energy in an engine, and the chemical energy in food is converted into the kinetic and potential energy of a person who climbs a flight of stairs. Radiant energy from the Sun is converted into electrical energy in a solar cell, and into chemical energy in a leaf by photosynthesis. Nuclear energy is converted into thermal energy in the core of a reactor, and then into electrical energy in the generator the steam turns. Thermal energy in the steam of a boiler is converted into the mechanical energy of a spinning turbine. Name the form you start from and the form you end at in each case, and say what does the converting.

exercises.prompt: List the energy conversions that occur when riding a bicycle.

answer.solution: The rider’s food is the source, so the chain begins with chemical energy in the muscles. That is converted into the mechanical work the legs do on the pedals, and about four fifths of it is converted into thermal energy in the rider at the same time, since cycling is about 20 percent efficient. The work on the pedals becomes the kinetic energy of the rider and the bicycle as they speed up, and becomes gravitational potential energy whenever the road climbs; coming down a hill that potential energy is converted back into kinetic energy. Friction in the chain and the bearings and the drag of the air convert part of the kinetic energy into thermal energy the whole time, which is why pedalling is needed to hold a steady speed on level ground. Braking converts the rest of the kinetic energy into thermal energy in the brake blocks and the rims. If the bicycle has a dynamo, a little of the mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy and then into the radiant energy of the lamp.

exercises.prompt: Using values from Table 7.1, how many DNA molecules could be broken by the energy carried by a single electron in the beam of an old-fashioned TV tube? (These electrons were not dangerous in themselves, but they did create dangerous x rays. Later model tube TVs had shielding that absorbed x rays before they escaped and exposed viewers.)

answer.hint: Read the energy of a single electron in the beam and the energy needed to break one DNA strand off Table 7.1, and divide the first by the second.

exercises.prompt: Using energy considerations and assuming negligible air resistance, show that a rock thrown from a bridge 20.0 m above water with an initial speed of 15.0 m/s strikes the water with a speed of 24.8 m/s independent of the direction thrown.

(a) Use of hydrogen fusion to supply energy is a dream that may be realized in the next century. Fusion would be a relatively clean and almost limitless supply of energy, as can be seen from Table 7.1. To illustrate this, calculate how many years the present energy needs of the world could be supplied by one millionth of the oceans’ hydrogen fusion energy. (b) How does this time compare with historically significant events, such as the duration of stable economic systems?

answer.hint: Table 7.1 gives the fusion energy of all the hydrogen in the oceans and the annual world energy use; take a millionth of the first and divide by the second.
answer.solution: (a) $25 \times 10^{6}\ \text{years}$ (b) This is much, much longer than human time scales.
